The girl under the tree tilted her head, silver hair sliding over the sharp red of her collar as she watched the flow of cars and suited office workers with the same idle interest one might give ants on a sidewalk. The halo above her cast a faint, wrong light in the shade, and the little smile on her lips said she was far more amused than lost.

When you had first approached, she’d looked you up and down in a single, precise sweep—shoes, face, the badge on your lanyard—then met your eyes as if she’d just decided something about you and filed it away. Her fingers toyed with the strap of the bag at her side, tapping an irregular rhythm like a fuse burning down.

“So,” she’d said, voice light, sing-songy, as though this were all part of a joke only she got, “this… isn’t any district I know. And you don’t look like a Prefect, a teacher, or a merc. Mm, but you do look… useful.” The last word had been stretched, teasing, as her eyes narrowed in faux-consideration. “Where exactly did I land, ‘useful person’?”

As the two of you stood beneath the tree by the curb, the air smelled faintly of exhaust and hot asphalt. Behind you, the office building’s glass facade reflected a dull sky and the steady trickle of employees returning from lunch. She seemed to drink it all in—the rumble of passing cars, the glow of phone screens, the lack of any other halos—masking a sharp, searching focus beneath lazy posture. Every time something unfamiliar passed—a delivery cyclist, a bus with an ad blaring across its side—her gaze flicked to it, catalogue-fast, before drifting back to you as if she hadn’t been paying attention at all.

Then a delivery truck turned too sharply into the narrow driveway beside the building.

The squeal of brakes tore across the parking lot, rubber screaming against pavement. The truck lurched, skidding just short of a parked car with a shudder that rattled its loose panels. A few people near the entrance jumped and swore; someone dropped their coffee. The driver slammed a hand on the steering wheel in frustrated relief.

Mutsuki didn’t flinch. Her eyes lit up.

“Oooh,” she murmured, grin stretching, the sound almost appreciative. “Now that’s familiar.” She glanced sidelong at you, as though checking how you reacted to the near-accident, then up at the confused cluster of office workers peering toward the driveway. “Tell me this place isn’t completely boring after all.”

Near the door, a uniformed security guard stepped out, frowning toward the truck. His gaze swept the area, following the small knot of people pointing and chattering—then snagged on the girl under the tree: the out-of-place uniform, the halo, the lazy, dangerous little smile.

His expression tightened. One hand went to the radio at his shoulder.

Mutsuki watched him notice her, the moment of suspicion landing, and her smile curved even further, almost delighted. Without looking away from the guard, she spoke to you in a low, amused tone.

“Mm. And now people with rules show up.” Her eyes sparkled. “So, ‘useful person’… what happens to strangers who don’t belong around here?”
